facts.statement: Adasaurus was a large dromaeosaurid measuring between 2.39 and 3.5 meters in length and weighing between 36.4 and 87 kilograms.
facts.quote: Adasaurus was a large dromaeosaurid that was about 2.39 - 3.5 m long weighing 36.4 - 87 kg.

facts.statement: Unlike other dromaeosaurids, Adasaurus possessed a small, blunt sickle claw with reduced use and a recurved lacrimal bone.
facts.quote: Unlike other dromaeosaurids, Adasaurus developed a rather small and blunt sickle claw that likely had a reduced use, and a recurved lacrimal bone

facts.statement: Adasaurus was first illustrated in 1977 by Rinchen Barsbold but remained an informally named taxon until its formal description.
facts.quote: Adasaurus was first figured in 1977 by the Mongolian paleontologist Rinchen Barsbold on a pelvic comparison with other theropods, but it would remain as an informally named taxon until a proper description.

facts.statement: Rinchen Barsbold formally named Adasaurus and its type species A. mongoliensis in 1983 based on two partial specimens.
facts.quote: In 1983, Barsbold published a large comparative revision of the known Mongolian theropod taxa at the time where he formally named Adasaurus and the type species A. mongoliensis, which was based on two partial specimens.

facts.statement: The name Adasaurus combines the Mongolian word for evil spirit and the Greek word for lizard.
facts.quote: The generic name, Adasaurus, is taken from the Mongolian word ад (ada, meaning evil spirit), and the Greek word σαῦρος (sauros, meaning lizard).

facts.statement: The holotype and paratype specimens of Adasaurus were unearthed from the Bügiin Tsav locality in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.
facts.quote: Both specimens were unearthed from the Nemegt Formation at the locality of Bügiin Tsav, in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.

facts.statement: In 2004, Philip J. Currie and David J. Varricchio referred two additional specimens to Adasaurus, though these were later found to belong to a different, older taxon.
facts.quote: In 2004, Philip J. Currie and David J. Varricchio referred another two specimens to Adasaurus labelled as IGM 100/22 and IGM 100/23.

facts.statement: In 2010, Phil Senter disputed the authenticity of the reduced sickle claw in Adasaurus, claiming the bone did not belong to the specimen.
facts.quote: However, the authenticity of this unusual reduction was disputed in 2010 by Phil Senter, who claimed that the supposed ungual did not pertain to the specimen.

facts.statement: Revisions indicate that Adasaurus belongs to the Velociraptorinae subfamily, which includes lightly built animals like Velociraptor.
facts.quote: Revisions made to the specimens have shown that this dromaeosaurid belongs to the Velociraptorinae, composed of more lightly-built animals like Velociraptor.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Adasaurus has an estimated length of 2.39 meters and a weight of 36.5 kilograms.
facts.quote: The holotype has an estimated length of 2.39 m with a weight of 36.5 kg.

facts.statement: The paratype specimen of Adasaurus is estimated to be around 3.5 meters long and 87 kilograms in body mass.
facts.quote: The comparatively larger pedal elements of the paratype indicate a gently bigger size in this latter specimen which is estimated around 3.5 m long and 87 kg in body mass.

facts.statement: The lacrimal bone in Adasaurus has an inverted L-shape with a curved thin body, a trait also seen in Austroraptor.
facts.quote: As in other dromaeosaurids, the lacrimal has an inverted L-shape, but the thin body of this bone is curved, which is also seen in Austroraptor.

facts.statement: In the holotype, the scapula and coracoid are completely fused into a scapulocoracoid with no visible suture between them.
facts.quote: The scapula and coracoid of the holotype are completely fused giving form to the scapulocoracoid, and the suture between them is not present.

facts.statement: The femur and tibia of the Adasaurus holotype measure 27.3 cm and 30.3 cm in length, respectively.
facts.quote: The femur and tibia of the holotype measure 27.3 cm and 30.3 cm long, respectively

facts.statement: The pubic peduncle in Adasaurus is wide and developed to the bottom, articulating with the pubis.
facts.quote: The pubic peduncle—a robust anterior extension that articulates with the pubis—is wide and developed to the bottom.

facts.statement: The second digit ungual in Adasaurus is not elongated like in most dromaeosaurids; its reduced size results in a metatarsal II-III ratio similar to Balaur.
facts.quote: The digit II ungual is not hypertrophied (elongated) as in most dromaeosaurids, and though Adasaurus features a similar metatarsal II-III ratio to that of Balaur, this is due to the reduced sickle claw of digit II instead of an elongated ungual of digit I.

facts.statement: Adasaurus is a member of Dromaeosauridae, a group closely related to living birds.
facts.quote: Adasaurus is a member of Dromaeosauridae, a group that is closely related to living birds.

facts.statement: While traditionally assigned to Dromaeosaurinae, several analyses suggest Adasaurus belongs to Velociraptorinae.
facts.quote: Traditionally, Adasaurus was assigned to the Dromaeosaurinae, which includes giant, heavily built animals such as Achillobator and Utahraptor but several analyses have suggested that it belongs to the Velociraptorinae instead.

facts.statement: Researchers in 2006 suggested that Adasaurus used its sickle claw less frequently than other deinonychosaurs due to the lack of asymmetrical ridges on its lower heel.
facts.quote: Kubota and Barsbold in 2006 stated that the highly reduced sickle claw of Adasaurus may have been used with less frequency than other deinonychosaurs

facts.statement: In 2011, Denver Fowler and colleagues proposed the 'Raptor Prey Restraint' model, suggesting dromaeosaurids pinned prey with their body weight and sickle claws before feeding.
facts.quote: In 2011, Denver Fowler and colleagues suggested a new method by which dromaeosaurids may have taken smaller prey.

facts.statement: Peter Bishop could not confirm or deny whether the sickle claw function was lost or retained in Adasaurus, noting its unusually small size and unique ginglymoid structure.
facts.quote: He could neither confirm nor disregard that the pedal digit II could have loss or retain its functionally.

facts.statement: Adasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 68 million years ago, in the Nemegt Formation.
facts.quote: Adasaurus is known from the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation, the age of which has been considered from the Late Campanian to Early-Middle Maastrichtian stages, about 70 million and 68 million years ago.

facts.statement: The environment of Adasaurus included stream channels, mudflats, and shallow lakes within the Nemegt Formation.
facts.quote: The environments that were present on the formation included stream and river channels, mudflats, and shallow lakes.

facts.statement: Adasaurus is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Dromaeosauridae

facts.statement: Adasaurus belongs to the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Dromaeosaurinae

facts.statement: Adasaurus mongoliensis is the only known species of the fossil dromaeosaurid genus Adasaurus, which lived in the Late Cretaceous of Asia.
facts.quote: Adasaurus mongoliensis ("lagarto de Ada de Mongolia") es la única especie conocida del género fósil Adasaurus de dinosaurio terópodo dromeosáurido que vivió en el Cretácico Superior, hace aproximadamente 70 million years ago en el Maastrichtiense, en lo que hoy es Asia.

facts.quote: Adasaurus, es único entre los dromeosáuridos, ya que la garra en hoz de sus pies son mucho más pequeñas.

facts.statement: Some estimates suggest Adasaurus was smaller, approximately 1.80 meters long, 70 centimeters high, and weighing about 15 kilograms.
